# Amazon VPC: say it

<!-- speak:start id=vpc-s01 -->
### Prompt 1

**A customer asks.** My worker only talks to S3. Why do I pay for a NAT gateway at all?

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**In 10 seconds.** For the S3 traffic, you shouldn't. A gateway endpoint carries it privately, with no hourly charge and no data processing charge.

**In 60 seconds.**

The short answer is: for the S3 traffic, you don't need the NAT gateway.

It works like this. A NAT gateway charges for every hour it runs.

It also charges for every gigabyte it processes, whatever the destination.

A gateway endpoint for S3 adds a route to the worker's route table.

Traffic to S3 matches that route, so it skips the NAT gateway.

And the endpoint has no hourly charge and no processing charge.

The thing to watch is that one endpoint serves one service.

If the worker calls S3 in its own Region alone, it needs no NAT gateway.

But software updates come from the internet, and need one.

In your case, I'd add the endpoint to the private route table between uploads.

Then the big uploads stop paying the NAT processing charge.

Which other hosts does the worker call, besides Amazon S3?

**Skeleton.** NAT bills hours and gigabytes / endpoint is a route / endpoint has no charge / updates still need NAT

**Must say.**

- A NAT gateway is charged for each hour that it is available and for each gigabyte of data that it processes.
- The data processing charge applies regardless of the traffic's source or destination, so S3 traffic through the NAT gateway is charged too.
- A gateway endpoint has no hourly charge and no data processing charge.
- Instances in subnets whose route table has the endpoint route use the gateway endpoint for the service automatically.

**Do not say.**

- "a gateway endpoint replaces the NAT gateway for all traffic". Say: A gateway endpoint reaches Amazon S3 and DynamoDB. Traffic to the internet still needs a NAT gateway.
- "S3 traffic through a NAT gateway is free because EC2 to S3 is free". Say: The NAT gateway charges data processing for every gigabyte, regardless of the traffic's source or destination.

**Follow-up questions.**

- Can our office network use the same endpoint to reach S3? No. Gateway endpoints do not allow access from on-premises networks, from peered VPCs in other Regions, or through a transit gateway. For those cases you use an interface endpoint, at an additional cost.
- Do we have to change the worker's code? No. Instances in subnets whose route table has the endpoint route automatically use the gateway endpoint. Instances in other subnets keep using the public service endpoint.

</details>
<!-- speak:end -->

<!-- speak:start id=vpc-s02 -->
### Prompt 2

**A customer asks.** Security group or network ACL: which one should protect my database?

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**In 10 seconds.** Both filter traffic. Start with the security group: it can allow only your app's security group. Add a network ACL to deny a source.

**In 60 seconds.**

Both are firewalls, but they sit at different levels.

The difference is what they remember, and whether they can deny.

It works like this. A security group sits on the database instance itself.

It has allow rules only, and it remembers each connection, so replies go back out.

Its rule can name your app's security group, not a list of addresses.

A network ACL sits on the whole subnet, with allow rules and deny rules.

The thing to watch is that a network ACL checks every packet, with no memory.

So you need rules for the replies too, or the connection breaks.

In your case, put the security group first, and keep the network ACL simple.

Do you need to block a known source, or only allow your application?

**Skeleton.** both firewalls, different levels / security group: allow only, stateful / network ACL: subnet, allow and deny / replies need network ACL rules

**Must say.**

- A security group works at the instance level; a network ACL works at the subnet level.
- A security group has allow rules only; a network ACL has allow and deny rules.
- A security group is stateful, so return traffic is allowed automatically; a network ACL is stateless, so return traffic must be explicitly allowed.
- The source of a security group rule can be the ID of another security group.

**Do not say.**

- "a security group can deny an IP address". Say: A security group has allow rules only. To deny a source, add a deny rule to a network ACL.
- "a network ACL remembers connections". Say: Network ACLs are stateless, so you must include a rule that allows responses to the inbound traffic.

**Follow-up questions.**

- If I remove a rule from the security group, does an open connection stop at once? No. Its tracked connections are not immediately interrupted; they continue until they time out. To interrupt the traffic at once, you can use a network ACL for the subnet.
- Does the network ACL filter traffic between the app and the database in the same subnet? No. Network ACLs do not filter traffic between instances in the same subnet. The security groups of the instances filter that traffic, because they work at the instance level.

</details>
<!-- speak:end -->

<!-- speak:start id=vpc-s03 -->
### Prompt 3

**A customer asks.** One NAT gateway in each Availability Zone, or one regional NAT gateway: what is the difference?

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**In 10 seconds.** Both keep outbound access when one Availability Zone fails. A regional NAT gateway follows your workloads and needs no public subnet.

**In 60 seconds.**

Both give your private subnets outbound access that survives an Availability Zone failure.

The difference is who places the gateways and the routes.

It works like this. A zonal NAT gateway lives in one Availability Zone.

So you create one per Availability Zone, each in a public subnet, with its own route.

A regional NAT gateway needs no public subnet.

It follows your workloads into each Availability Zone, and every subnet uses one route.

The thing to watch is billing: it's charged for each Availability Zone where it runs.

It also doesn't support private NAT.

And reaching a new Availability Zone can take up to sixty minutes.

In your case, a regional NAT gateway means less routing work for your team.

Do any of your private subnets need private NAT to reach another network?

**Skeleton.** both survive an AZ failure / zonal: one per AZ, public subnet / regional: follows workloads, one route / billed per AZ, no private NAT

**Must say.**

- A zonal NAT gateway is created in one Availability Zone and is redundant inside that zone.
- If several zones share one zonal NAT gateway and its zone fails, resources in the other Availability Zones lose internet access, so you create one per zone.
- A regional NAT gateway automatically expands across Availability Zones based on where your workloads are.
- A regional NAT gateway needs no public subnet and uses one NAT ID across Availability Zones, so subnets can share one route entry.
- A regional NAT gateway is charged for each hour that it is configured in each Availability Zone.

**Do not say.**

- "a regional NAT gateway has one hourly charge for all zones". Say: A regional NAT gateway is charged for each hour that it is configured in each Availability Zone.
- "a regional NAT gateway supports private NAT". Say: Regional NAT gateways do not support private NAT. Use a zonal NAT gateway for private NAT.
- "one zonal NAT gateway is highly available for every zone". Say: A zonal NAT gateway is redundant inside its own zone. If that zone fails, resources in the other Availability Zones lose internet access.

**Follow-up questions.**

- How many connections can a NAT gateway handle to one busy destination? Each IP address supports 55,000 simultaneous connections to one destination. A zonal NAT gateway takes up to 8 IPv4 addresses. A regional one supports 32 IP addresses per Availability Zone.
- When we launch instances in a new zone, is the regional NAT gateway there right away? Not always. It can take up to 60 minutes to expand to a new Availability Zone. Until then, the gateway in an existing zone handles that traffic across zones.

</details>
<!-- speak:end -->

<!-- speak:start id=vpc-s04 -->
### Prompt 4

**A customer asks.** There is a line on our bill for public IP addresses. Do our servers need them?

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**In 10 seconds.** Only the web instance that customers visit needs one. Each public address is billed every hour, in use or idle.

**In 60 seconds.**

The short answer is: only the web instance that customers visit needs one.

It works like this. A public IP address lets the internet reach one instance.

AWS charges for each one by the hour, whether it's in use or idle.

The worker and the database don't need to be reached from the internet.

So they move to a private subnet, a part the internet cannot reach.

They still reach the internet for updates through a NAT gateway.

That's a shared exit: they can go out, but nobody can come in.

The thing to watch is the NAT gateway's own hourly charge and address.

In your case, the web instance keeps its address, and the NAT gateway has its own.

Which of your instances must customers reach directly?

**Skeleton.** only the web instance / billed hourly, used or idle / private subnet plus NAT gateway / NAT gateway: hours, gigabytes, its address

**Must say.**

- You pay an hourly rate for each public IPv4 address, and the price is the same whether the address is in use or idle.
- An instance that does not need to be reached directly from the internet should not be in a public subnet.
- Instances without public IP addresses reach the internet through a NAT gateway, and hosts on the internet cannot start a connection to them.
- A NAT gateway is charged for each hour that it is available and for each gigabyte of data that it processes.
- A public NAT gateway has an Elastic IP address, and every public IPv4 address is billed.

**Do not say.**

- "Elastic IP addresses are free while they are attached". Say: An Elastic IP address is a public IPv4 address, and every public IPv4 address is billed hourly, in use or idle.
- "private instances cannot download updates". Say: Private instances reach the internet through a NAT gateway. The NAT gateway allows outbound connections and blocks connections started from the internet.

**Follow-up questions.**

- If the web instance needs an address that never changes, what do we use? An Elastic IP address. It remains allocated to your account until you explicitly release it. It is billed like any other public IPv4 address, in use or idle.
- Can the database still download its updates without a public address? Yes. Instances without public IP addresses route their traffic through a NAT gateway to reach the internet. Hosts on the internet cannot start a connection to them.

</details>
<!-- speak:end -->
